records.question: Under Erie Railroad Co. v. Tompkins, must a US federal court that hears a state-law claim in diversity jurisdiction apply federal general common law?
records.answer: Nah, that doesn't work like that. Under Erie Railroad Co. v. Tompkins, a federal court hearing a state-law claim under diversity jurisdiction must apply the relevant state's substantive law, not federal general common law. ❌
records.why: The Erie Railroad Co. v. Tompkins decision explicitly overruled Swift v. Tyson and held that there is no federal general common law. Federal courts in diversity cases must apply the substantive law of the state, including its common law, as declared by its legislature or highest court, except where federal constitutional provisions or Acts of Congress control.

records.question: Can Parliament use Article 368 to amend the basic structure of the Indian Constitution?
records.answer: Nah, that doesn't work like that. Parliament cannot use Article 368 to amend or destroy the basic structure of the Indian Constitution; this limitation was established by the Supreme Court in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973). ❌
records.why: The Kesavananda Bharati judgment, as published on Indian Kanoon and the Supreme Court's official website, is the primary source establishing that while Article 368 grants Parliament broad amending power, this power is constrained by the basic structure doctrine and cannot be used to alter or destroy the Constitution's basic structure. The judgment was delivered by a 13-judge bench with a 7-6 majority on April 24, 1973, and has been consistently upheld in subsequent cases like Minerva Mills.

records.question: Which section of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 currently punishes theft?
records.answer: Section 379 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 prescribed the punishment for theft as imprisonment of either description for a term extending to three years, or with fine, or with both. ⚖️
records.why: The IndiaCode eCourts page for IPC Section 379 confirms the heading 'Punishment for theft' and the penalty: imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. The Ministry of Home Affairs press release confirms the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 came into force on 1 July 2024. Section 358(1) of the BNS repeals the IPC, and Section 303 of the BNS now governs theft.

records.question: What penalty does India's Digital India Act impose for a personal data breach?
records.answer: The enacted Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (DPDP Act) provides for penalties under its Schedule: up to ₹250 crore for failing to implement reasonable security safeguards to prevent a personal data breach, and up to ₹200 crore for failing to notify the Data Protection Board or affected individuals of a breach, with the exact amount determined by the Data Protection Board following an inquiry. ⚖️
records.why: The Digital India Act remains a proposal and has not been enacted, so it imposes no penalties. The DPDP Act, 2023 is the enacted legislation governing personal data breaches, with its Schedule specifying maximum penalties of ₹250 crore for inadequate security safeguards and ₹200 crore for failure to notify, subject to adjudication by the Data Protection Board under section 33.
caveats: One part of this is not confirmed: Section 33(2) of the DPDP Act identifies factors relevant to determining the amount of penalties.

records.question: Can material licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 be included in a program that is distributed under the GNU GPL version 3?
records.answer: Nah, that doesn't work like that. Material licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 cannot be incorporated into an adapted or combined work distributed under GNU GPL version 3, because Creative Commons has not designated GPLv3 as a compatible license for CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. ❌
records.why: The CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license includes a ShareAlike condition (section 3(b)(1)) that requires adaptations to be licensed under the same license, a later version, a ported version, or a license specifically designated as compatible by Creative Commons. The official Creative Commons compatible licenses list shows that no non-Creative Commons licenses, including GPLv3, have been designated as compatible with CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. Therefore, distributing an adaptation of CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 material under GPLv3 violates the license terms.
caveats: One part of this is not confirmed: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 material incorporated into an adapted or combined work distributed under GNU GPL version 3...

records.question: Is training a generative AI model on copyrighted books without a licence fair use under US law?
records.answer: Yeah, you're right. Training a generative AI model on copyrighted books without a licence is not automatically fair use under US law; it depends on a case-specific four-factor analysis, and while some courts have found certain training uses to be fair use, no blanket rule exists. ✅
records.why: The US Copyright Act's fair use provision (17 U.S.C. § 107) requires a four-factor analysis for any use, including AI training. The Bartz v. Anthropic case demonstrates that courts apply this test to AI training, finding some uses (like model training) to be fair use while rejecting others (like building a pirated library). No statute or ruling creates a blanket exception for AI training.
caveats: The Bartz decision is a single district court ruling and not binding precedent; other courts may reach different conclusions.
